Back to index

What this is. Output of the SF++ set-reconciliation simulator in NomDeTom/Meshtasticatom, built from the run digests on its sim-results branch by a scheduled job. Nothing on this page is hand-written or hand-edited.

What it is not. Not a measurement of a real network. The radio model, terrain and clutter come from Meshtasticator and Komzpa's terrain stack; the mesh, traffic and archive behaviour are simulated. held and union are what an archive holds, not what a user receives.

Reading it. The four delivery measures have four different denominators and are not comparable to each other. demand is aggregate airtime demand across the whole mesh, a multiple with no ceiling; chutil is what a device reports and cannot exceed 100%.

Licence. This page is output of the simulator in NomDeTom/Meshtasticatom, which is distributed under GPL-3.0 because parts of it are transcribed from Meshtastic firmware. A program's output is not the program: this page describes a simulation and is free to read and quote. The simulator's Meshtasticator half remains CC BY 4.0, attribution preserved. Part of that simulator's source is based on Spinsante, Gioacchini and Scalise, A novel experimental-based tool for the design of LoRa networks (MetroInd4.0&IoT, 2019), which stems from Bor, Roedig, Voigt and Alonso, Do LoRa Low-Power Wide-Area Networks Scale? (MSWiM '16) and the LoRaSim library. Terrain, clutter and the capture-aware physics are from Komzpa's Meshtasticator branch.

SF++ sweep explorer

5 scheduled run(s), 104 block(s), rolling. Each column is one run: one random seed base over one landform.

5 runs first blocks-2026-08-27-3444599 latest matrix-2026-08-28-1538 ground batumi, flat, ridge transport 4195f52 sim 1.6.1

24 earlier run(s) are excluded from every metric below: they were measured before sim 1.6.1, which changed what the numbers mean. They still appear under run health, whose costs remain comparable.

215 mesh recipe(s)516 block(s)

The mesh every block below was run on, and how it was made. Every number on this page is conditional on this: a reach figure is a statement about this mesh at this hop limit, and two recipes are two experiments rather than two cells.

What moves a delivery measure

Mean spread of the measure each block moves most, averaged over the runs that carry it. The four measures have four denominators and are not comparable to each other - measure names which one this block travels in. A large text spread beside it means the block decides its measure by spending the mesh's own broadcast reach.

batumi-x4-LONG_FAST

placementbatumi1 run(s)tracking held

Batumi mirrored into four reflected copies - 368 nodes over the same terrain, so size moves and the ground does not. Three-quarters of the resulting pairs fall outside the fitted link budget, so read pairs_beyond_calibration before anything else here, on LONG_FAST, the shipped default and the middle of the deployed range. Crossed against the archive off and at every placement and count, so the capping of the role-bounded placements is visible rather than hidden.

batumi-x4-SHORT_FAST

placementbatumi1 run(s)tracking held

Batumi mirrored into four reflected copies - 368 nodes over the same terrain, so size moves and the ground does not. Three-quarters of the resulting pairs fall outside the fitted link budget, so read pairs_beyond_calibration before anything else here, on SHORT_FAST, the fast end of what deployed meshes run: least airtime per packet and the least range per hop, so the mesh is quiet but sparser. Crossed against the archive off and at every placement and count, so the capping of the role-bounded placements is visible rather than hidden.

Chart explorer

Any number of measures, drawn for every block that records them, on a single scale. The per-block charts each scale to their own numbers - right for reading one block, wrong for comparing two, since a 0.09 bar and a 0.87 bar both reach the top of their own chart. Whiskers are one standard deviation across the seeds of that cell: where two of them overlap, the arm has not moved the measure by more than the draw did.

measures
blocks

This page draws from the same digest numbers as the tables; it needs JavaScript.

Schedule

Every cell the tree declares, against the runs in this archive. Two different readings of “still to do” and they disagree by design: the block sweep runs nightly and touches all 87 every night, while the matrix and the cross run weekly and touch a cell once a week - so not in the latest run means something for the first and nothing for the other two. runs counts every run a cell appears in; never is the column that means work outstanding.

AD-amplifiers2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noPower amplifiers as separate transmit and receive gain, sprinkled or in an arms race.
AD-amplify-worst2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noA high amplifier fitted to the worst-connected nodes after the links exist - the field pathology where the node nobody could hear is then heard by everyone while still hearing almost nobody.
AD-badrouters2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noWhere the router roles land - on the best-connected nodes, the worst, or at random.
AD-flooding2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noEvery node rebroadcasting everything, against a real role census.
AD-nomute2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe role census: a real mesh's mix, the same without muted clients, and everything a router.
AD-siting2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noSiting against a real role census, including a basement-heavy mesh.
AD-worst2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noRouter roles on the worst-connected nodes of an already badly sited mesh - the adversarial case.
BL-control2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe same nodes in the same places with the archive off then on, separating what serving costs a node from where it sits.
DB-hotstore2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe modelled MAX_NUM_NODES - the size of the hot store.
DB-hotstore-stress2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe store size against a fixed 250-node mesh, so eviction is constant.
DB-platform2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe board mix, which decides each node's hot-store size.
DB-warm2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe warm tier on a mesh larger than the hot store: 0 is the pre-2.8 behaviour of forgetting an evicted peer outright.
DG-burst2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe same nominal loss delivered in 60-second stretches of deafness, which puts a whole bucket's divergence into one sketch instead of spreading it.
DG-loss2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noA flat loss floor on every reception - degradation spread evenly across every bucket.
DG-outage2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noBurst loss at half an hour rather than a minute - most of a bucket, which is the outage that actually matters to an archive.
DM-mode2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noHow a DM escalates to flooding.
FW-firmware2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe pre-fold-in transport against 2.8 - same seed, same mesh, only the MAC and routing rules change.
FW-mixed2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noA mesh part-way through upgrading, the older share on 2.5.
FW-mixed-262blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe same with the older share on 2.6.
FW-signing-cost2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noSigning itself, on against off inside 2.8. The only arm that separates 'signing costs reach' from '2.8 costs reach'.
FW-versions2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe release series in order, each at its final release - what a mesh gained or lost per upgrade, not what one rule is worth.
LD-chatty2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe device broadcast interval driven down to three times its default rate.
LD-chatty-hops2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe same, with every node on a flat hop limit of 7 so nothing damps the flood.
LD-diurnal2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noTime of day. Text, position and DMs follow the clock; telemetry and nodeinfo are device timers and do not.
LD-interval2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe device broadcast interval - the denominator every SF++ airtime share is quoted against.
LD-traceroute2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noRoute discoveries per node per hour - whether traceroute learning pays for its own airtime.
LD-traceroute-small2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe same on a mesh whose hot store cannot hold it, where the overflow cache is all that keeps a route for the long tail.
MS-density2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe same node counts in a fixed area, so this is density rather than size. Running both is the only way to say which an effect belongs to.
MS-hopscale2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noHow far the firmware's hop estimator sits from the exhaustive count it approximates, as the mesh outgrows its 128 entries.
MS-oversubscribed2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noMesh size against a store that has to hold it, over a full day.
MS-roles2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe legacy default role census against a real mesh's.
MS-roles-fav2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe same with router favourites on.
MS-router-late2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe share of nodes on ROUTER_LATE.
MS-siting2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noWhere nodes physically are. A roof node and a basement one are 26 dB apart, wider than most parameters here.
MS-size2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noMesh size with density held constant - the area grows with the node count.
MS-stretch2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noEvery distance scaled about the centroid: the same nodes in the same arrangement, further apart.
MS-topology2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe shape of the mesh, at fixed node count and seed.
PR-crladder2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noRaising the coding rate on each retransmission - airtime spent to make each attempt likelier to land.
PR-dmmode-cr2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noDM escalation with the coding-rate ladder already on, since both spend the same retry budget.
PR-protocol2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noNothing, the incumbent chain walk, and the sketch - with `none` a paired baseline, so every other cell is a difference rather than a comparison.
PR-repeats2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe cheapest rival to an archive: one extra relay of a text rather than replicating it afterwards.
PR-repeats-busy2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe same, on a mesh busy enough for the suppression thresholds to be deciding it.
RF-bw5002blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noSpreading factor with bandwidth held at 500 kHz, where North America is heading.
RF-duct2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noTropospheric ducting episodes per hour. Not a free gain - read ducted receptions beside collisions.
RF-eu-presets2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe presets Europe runs, including the narrow ones EU_866 and EU_N_868 default to.
RF-noise2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe noise floor: none, a smooth field, episodic bursts, or a regular emitter that wipes whatever is in flight.
RF-preset2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe presets deployed meshes actually run: the default, the fast end, and the slow end still in use.
RF-preset-turbo2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noPresets from the fastest the firmware ships to the slow end.
RF-pulse2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noHow often the periodic emitter fires.
RF-stretch-duct2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noDucting on a stretched mesh, where the long links it creates are the ones that were missing.
RF-txpower2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noTransmit power in dBm - the region limit is a ceiling an operator may use, not one they must.
RT-adopt2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe hop-recommendation feedback loop closed against held open, traced, because a converged mean and an oscillating one look identical at the end.
RT-favourites2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noRouter-like nodes favouriting each other, so relays between them keep their hop limit.
RT-hopassign2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noWhether raised hop limits land on central nodes as operators do it, or at random - the control that separates the limit's effect from the siting of the nodes that raised it.
RT-hoplimit2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noHop limits past anything a release ships, to find where more hops stop helping.
RT-hopspread2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noOne hop limit for everyone, swept. The per-node spread must be off or --hop-limit is never read.
RT-rebroadcast2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe rebroadcast mode - what a node relays.
RT-spread2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noA uniform hop limit against per-node limits of 3-7 assigned by centrality.
SC-signing2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe receive-side signature policy - what a node does with an unsigned packet.
SF-advert-transport2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noWhether an archive advertises by broadcast or by DM to each known peer.
SF-bucket-mode2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noWhat defines a bucket: a global counter (a fiction kept as an upper bound), the local count the firmware keeps, a time window, or a sliding window.
SF-bucket-time2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noWidth of the time bucket, when buckets are cut by the clock.
SF-cadence2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noWhen an archive advertises: on a sealed bucket, a fixed interval, AIMD, or both.
SF-capacity2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noHow many differences one sketch can decode before it fails and the exchange escalates.
SF-capacity-local2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noSketch capacity under local numbering and the later defaults.
SF-capacity-window2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noSketch capacity under windowed buckets rather than counted ones.
SF-catchup2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe quiet-hours window reconciliation defers to, which only means anything once traffic has a time of day.
SF-hops-flat2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noHow many hops apart the archives are placed, under a flat hop limit.
SF-hops-spread2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noHow many hops apart the archives are, under real per-node hop limits.
SF-jitter-global2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noSpread applied to bucket-close under global numbering, where every archive seals the same bucket at the same moment and fires together.
SF-jitter-local2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noAdvert spread under local numbering, where each archive seals its own bucket on its own count and the synchronisation jitter would break is largely absent.
SF-place-flat2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noWhere the archives sit, under a flat hop limit.
SF-place-spread2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noWhere the archives sit, under real per-node hop limits.
SF-provide-transport2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noWhether a replay goes by DM or by broadcast, so bystanders in earshot can file it too.
SF-replay-order2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noWhere a replayed object lands in the receiver's stream: at the tip, or back at its heard_ago.
SF-replay-order-broadcast2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe same, with replays broadcast - the combination the replay header exists for.
SF-resolve2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noHow two archives settle a disagreement - send a sketch, enumerate, or sketch then fall back. Delivery should not move; what it costs should.
SF-servers-allrouters2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noEvery router as an archive against half of them - same mesh, same traffic, only who holds the archive changes.
SF-servers-flat2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noHow many archives the mesh has, under a flat hop limit.
SF-servers-spread2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noHow many archives the mesh has, under real per-node hop limits.
SF-signed2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noWhether the advert carries its 66-byte signature.
SF-sr-retries2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noRetries per addressed reconciliation hop, to find where delivery stops improving.
SF-width2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noSketch member width. Narrower identifiers collide more often, and a collision cancels in the sketch without cancelling in the checksum.
SF-window-size2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noObjects in the sliding window, when buckets are windowed.
TH-congestion2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noThe firmware's node-count interval scaling, on against off.
TH-congestion-input2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noWhich quantity drives the throttle: what the firmware can see and which saturates, or the unbounded ideal.
TH-congestion-mode2blocks-2026-08-28-4161552noEach node throttling on its own online count against one coefficient for the whole mesh. The firmware does the former.

batumi-coding-rate-laddernever-nothe 92-node Batumi snapshot on its own ground, at the shipped defaults; each retransmission goes out at a higher coding rate - more redundancy and more airtime per attempt. Not in any release. Crossed against the archive off and at every placement and count.
batumi-congestion-40never-nothe 92-node Batumi snapshot on its own ground, at the shipped defaults; broadcast intervals still start stretching above 40 nodes, the firmware's own constant. This arm must reproduce the unchanged mesh exactly. Crossed against the archive off and at every placement and count.
batumi-congestion-60never-nothe 92-node Batumi snapshot on its own ground, at the shipped defaults; broadcast intervals hold their shipped cadence up to 60 nodes before stretching, so the mesh stays chattier for longer. Crossed against the archive off and at every placement and count.
batumi-congestion-80never-nothe 92-node Batumi snapshot on its own ground, at the shipped defaults; broadcast intervals hold their shipped cadence up to 80 nodes - on a mesh this size, almost no throttling at all. Crossed against the archive off and at every placement and count.
batumi-extra-repeatsnever-nothe 92-node Batumi snapshot on its own ground, at the shipped defaults; a node tolerates a second heard copy before cancelling its own rebroadcast, so a text is relayed more often. Not in any release. Crossed against the archive off and at every placement and count.
batumi-favourite-routersnever-nothe 92-node Batumi snapshot on its own ground, at the shipped defaults; router-like nodes favourite each other, so a relay between two of them keeps its hop limit instead of spending one. Crossed against the archive off and at every placement and count.
batumi-hop-limit-15never-nothe 92-node Batumi snapshot on its own ground, at the shipped defaults; every node at 15 hops - a ceiling far past anything this mesh can use, which is the point: it shows what the limit was costing when it bound. Crossed against the archive off and at every placement and count.
batumi-hop-limit-7never-nothe 92-node Batumi snapshot on its own ground, at the shipped defaults; every node at 7 hops instead of the per-node 3-7 by centrality. Crossed against the archive off and at every placement and count.
batumi-x4-nonenever-noBatumi mirrored into four reflected copies - four times the nodes over the same terrain, so size moves and the ground does not. Seam-spanning pairs sit outside the fitted link budget; read pairs_beyond_calibration before anything else; nothing changed - the mesh as the firmware ships it. Crossed against the archive off and at every placement and count.

batumi-x1-LITE_FAST1matrix-2026-08-28-1538yesthe 92-node Batumi snapshot on its own ground, on LITE_FAST, the EU_866 default - a narrower 125 kHz channel that buys sensitivity back at four times LONG_FAST's airtime. Crossed against the archive off and at every placement and count, so the capping of the role-bounded placements is visible rather than hidden.
batumi-x1-LONG_FAST1matrix-2026-08-28-1538yesthe 92-node Batumi snapshot on its own ground, on LONG_FAST, the shipped default and the middle of the deployed range. Crossed against the archive off and at every placement and count, so the capping of the role-bounded placements is visible rather than hidden.
batumi-x1-SHORT_FASTnever-nothe 92-node Batumi snapshot on its own ground, on SHORT_FAST, the fast end of what deployed meshes run: least airtime per packet and the least range per hop, so the mesh is quiet but sparser. Crossed against the archive off and at every placement and count, so the capping of the role-bounded placements is visible rather than hidden.

Run health

What each run cost and what it flagged. Duration is given both ways on purpose. compute h is what the run actually spent, which is what decides whether a job fits its ceiling; s/sim-h is wall-clock seconds per simulated hour, the only form comparable between runs of different length - and the form the digest gates on, because the total moves whenever --hours or the seed count does. Flag kinds are counted, not ranked: beyond-envelope on a mirrored cell is expected by construction, and colouring every warning red would train everyone to skip them.

How these runs are made

Everything here is written by scheduled workflows into one archive branch, and this page is rebuilt from that archive. They ask two different kinds of question, which is why one block list holds two naming conventions: a synthetic mesh moving one flag at a time, and a real mesh over real ground. The last section is the glossary: what every column on this page actually counts, and what it is counted against.

  1. The mechanism sweep
  2. Real ground
  3. What joins them up
  4. What each term means

1. The mechanism sweep

synthetic meshnightly 02:10 UTCruns/blocks-<date>-<seed>

What does this one variable do to a mesh? Every block sfpp.sweep declares - 87 of them - against a generated mesh, with one landform and one seed base drawn for the whole night so every block that night saw the same draw. One arm moves per block; everything else is held. Each block is its own job, because a single job running all 87 in sequence is about six hours of simulator time and one slow block would take the night down with it.

Cells are named <DD>-subject - a two-letter domain and a kebab tail, RF-preset-turbo, SF-capacity, DG-outage. The archive is switched on in every cell, so this style can say what a variable does and can never say what the archive itself is worth.

2. Real ground

Batumi, real geometry and terraintwo workflowsruns/matrix-<date>, runs/design-<date>-<seed>

Both run over a real node snapshot with matching terrain, so their cells are named for the ground rather than a domain: batumi-x1-LONG_FAST, batumi-coding-rate-ladder - scenario, mirror count, then the thing being varied. They predate the domain scheme and are not governed by it.

They are heavier than the mechanism sweep: the link build is O(n²) with a terrain profile and a clutter walk per pair, so a mirrored cell spends most of its time before the simulation starts. Neither runs its whole grid nightly - each night takes the stalest cells it has not covered recently, so a full pass completes over roughly a week.

Sim Sweep (matrix) · 03:40 UTC · three presets, two scales, three placements, three archive counts, five seeds, with a no-archive baseline per seed per scale. Asks whether a preset ordering survives scaling, and whether any deliberate placement beats picking nodes at random.

Sim Design (cross) · 04:40 UTC · a three-axis cross: what the archive is configured as, against what could be deployed instead of it, on each mesh in the round. This is the one that can answer what the archive is worth, because the archive sits on an axis rather than being on everywhere.

What joins them up

Sim Collate is called by all three rather than scheduled. It reduces a run to the two files this page reads - summary.json and trend.md - and applies the standing gates, so a run that produced an impossible number is caught where it was made.

Sim Results Explorer rebuilds this page at 06:20 UTC, after all three producers have finished. It reads only the digests, never the raw block JSONs, so the archive can drop raw runs without the page losing its history - and a figure that lives beside a dropped JSON can never be shown here at all, which is why the charts are drawn in the browser from numbers embedded in the page.

What each term means

every column on this pagefour denominators

Four questions, four denominators, and they are not comparable to each other. A DM figure higher than a text figure does not mean DMs work better - a DM needs to reach one node and gets retries, while text reach is the share of all nodes that heard it.

columnwhat it countsout of
delivery - what arrived, and by which route
textshare of broadcast texts a node holds, however it got there - the on-air and overheard columns below sum to thisevery node, every broadcast text
on airof those, what the broadcast itself delivered. First chance. This is the one to quote when asking whether the mesh got better, and it is what an arm is priced againstevery node, every broadcast text
overheardof those, what was filed from an overheard replay - a bystander keeping an archived object it was never sent, because the replay header sits outside the encryption wrapper. Zero for a protocol that puts no replay on the airevery node, every broadcast text
worst nodethe least-served node's text reach. Prefer it to the mean: the mean is carried by the middle of a mesh, and the archive argument is about the edgeone node, every broadcast text
DMdid the direct message reach the one node it was addressed to? A bystander hearing it relayed it; that is not deliveryDMs that reached the air
admindid the operator's change take, within the attempts they made? Both legs - the request and the reply - must land inside the firmware's 300 s windowsessions the operator wanted
inventory - what an archive has
heldwhat one archive holds, averaged over the archives. Not a delivery measure: there is no client hydration path, so nothing here models a user asking a server for what they missedobjects originated
unionwhat all archives together hold - the ceiling reconciliation is working towards. A high union beside a low held means the copies have divergedobjects originated
cost - what it spent to get there
demandevery node's transmit time summed over elapsed time - aggregate demand, not a busy fraction. Unbounded: above 1.0 is normal, because spatial reuse means most transmissions never overlap at any one receiverelapsed time (1.0 = one channel-second asked for per second)
chutil p90/maxAirTime::channelUtilizationPercent per node - what a real device reports and what sizes its contention window. Quote this one when asking whether a mesh is busywall-clock, per node (0-100%)
airutil maxnode_air_util_tx_percent: what the busiest node would have to declare as its own transmit dutywall-clock, per node (0-100%)
SR airreconciliation's share of all channel airtime - the archive's bill, separated from the traffic it is carried alongsidetotal airtime on the mesh
priceon the ranking table: how much more of something an arm spent across its cells, as a ratio - bytes on air, advert bytes or SR bytes, whichever moved furthestthe arm's own lowest cell
the run itself
placedarchives actually sited against the number asked for. A role-bounded placement quietly returning fewer is how “6 servers” and “4 servers” become one rowarchives requested
movedon the ranking table: which delivery measure this block travels in. The four have four denominators and are not comparable to each other-
spreadthe distance between the arm's lowest and highest cell on whichever measure it moved - how much the variable is worth at all-
cellshow many values of the arm this block ran. A block with two cells states a difference; one with six states a shape-

Every per-node quantity on this page is reported as min / p10 / median / mean / p90 / max. The mean alone cannot say whether a mesh serves its worst node, which is the question the archive exists to answer.

How SF++ works

Store & Forward++ gives some nodes an archive: a store of the broadcast text objects that crossed the mesh, so a node that was off, asleep or out of range can be caught up afterwards. Two archives that have seen different traffic hold different sets, and the whole protocol is the problem of finding the difference between two sets over a radio that carries a few hundred bytes at a time. What follows is how it does that today, and what is proposed instead.

  1. The shape of the problem
  2. Today: the chain walk
  3. Proposed: set reconciliation
  4. The knobs, and what each decides
  5. Replays, and who else hears them

1. The shape of the problem

why it is not just "send me what I missed"

An archive cannot ask for what it missed, because it does not know what it missed. It knows what it holds. So does its peer. Neither can send its whole list - a mesh packet carries a couple of hundred bytes and a store holds thousands of objects - and neither can ask a question whose answer is the list either.

Both forms below start from the same two primitives. An object is identified by a message hash, and a set of them by a checksum that is order-independent, so two archives holding the same objects agree on it whatever order they arrived in. The checksum settles whether two archives differ in one small message. Everything expensive is the second question: which objects.

2. Today: the chain walk

--protocol chainshipped

Each archive keeps its objects as a chain: every object commits to the one before it, so the store is an ordered list ending in a tip. Three messages:

messagewhat it carriessize
CANON_ANNOUNCEbroadcast: this archive's tip - a commit hash and a counter. Cheap, and it does not grow with how far behind anyone is28 B
LINK_REQUESTaddressed: name one commit I want24 B
LINK_PROVIDEthe object, plus the hash of its parent44 B + object

A node hearing a tip it does not hold asks for it. The answer carries the object and the parent's hash - which is the only way it learns what to ask for next. So it asks again, and again, walking backwards one object per round trip until it reaches something it already has.

A difference of d objects costs d round trips, and they cannot be pipelined, because each request is only knowable once the previous answer has arrived. That serialisation is the cost, and on a mesh whose diameter is nineteen hops every one of those round trips crosses the whole line. Measured here: chain spends about 70% of its bytes on negotiation rather than on objects.

3. Proposed: set reconciliation

--protocol srunder study

Replace the walk with one exchange. Objects are grouped into buckets, and for each bucket an archive computes a sketch - a fixed-size structure, sized by --capacity, over the short IDs of the objects it holds. The advert is a broadcast carrying the bucket, its checksum, and that sketch.

A peer hearing it does three things in order:

  1. Compare checksums. Equal means the sets are identical and the exchange is over - one message, no round trip.
  2. Subtract the sketches. The sketch is built so that combining two of them cancels everything the two archives share and leaves only the symmetric difference, which decodes directly to the short IDs neither side has in common - without either side ever sending its list.
  3. Answer both halves at once. IDs it holds and the peer lacks it sends; IDs it lacks it asks for in a single request. One exchange, whatever d is - up to the sketch's capacity.

The capacity is the catch. A sketch of capacity c can only decode a difference of at most c; beyond that it fails - detectably - and the exchange escalates to enumeration, which is a round trip longer but always works. That is what --resolve hybrid is: sketch first, enumerate when it fails. Measured here, the decode failure rate is not small at slow cadence - a third of exchanges at bucket-close, because rare adverts mean big differences.

Sketch bytes are capacity x short-ID bits / 8: at the defaults, 32 members of 32 bits is 128 bytes on top of an 18-byte envelope and a 9-byte checksum. The trade is bytes per advert against round trips per object, and that is the whole comparison this campaign exists to measure.

4. The knobs, and what each decides

knobdecidesvalues
--resolvehow the difference is found once two archives know they differsketch only, enum only (never sends a sketch; a round trip longer by design), hybrid - sketch, escalating on failure
--triggerwhen an archive speaks at allbucket on a seal, interval on a timer, aimd backing off when a probe finds nothing
--capacitythe largest difference one sketch can decode, and most of the advert's size32 by default
--bucket-modehow objects are grouped so two archives can talk about the same subsetlocal is what the firmware does; the others need agreement no mesh can produce
--short-id-bitshow wide a member of the sketch is - narrower is cheaper and collides more32 by default

Cadence is the one that moves everything: advertise rarely and differences grow past the sketch capacity, advertise often and the archive's own traffic is most of what the channel carries. Both ends of that are measured in the cadence blocks.

5. Replays, and who else hears them

When an archive sends an object it has that a peer lacks, that is a replay. It carries a small header - how long ago the object was first heard, in 64-second ticks - and that header sits outside the encryption wrapper. Its presence is the flag: fresh traffic carries none.

So any node in earshot, archive or not, can tell that what it is hearing is a replay and roughly how old it is, and can file it as a message it missed. That is a bystander pickup, and it is the only end-user gain this campaign measures: nothing here models a client asking a server for what it missed, so held is what an archive has, not what a user gets.

It is also why every reach figure on this page is split into on air and overheard. A protocol that puts more replays on the air is overheard more, regardless of whether it reconciles well - the chain walk is overheard about twice as much as the sketch, and it is the worse reconciler.
